title: A City in a City for Renters
hook: A New York insurance giant laid out a renters' utopia on an old golf course, with streets named after Anza's colonists and courtyards meant for highballs.
story: Having ridden out the Depression, the Metropolitan Life Insurance Company decided rental housing was a steadier bet. After Parkchester in the Bronx and Park La Brea in Los Angeles, in 1941 it bought almost 200 acres beside Lake Merced from the Spring Valley Water Company [1]. Met Life promised that only 18 percent of the land would be built on; the rest would be gardens and play fields [1]. Architects Leonard Schultze and Associates brought in landscape architect Thomas Dolliver Church, and they drew pie-shaped blocks radiating from Juan Bautista Circle, with avenues named for members of the 1775–76 Anza expedition [1][2]. War rationing forced a switch from steel to wood frame, but the first tenants moved into Font Boulevard garden apartments in early 1944, paying $52 to $84.50 a month [1]. A 1949 permit added eleven thirteen-story towers, the tallest buildings west of Twin Peaks [1]. One reviewer, Mark Daniels, praised the private front terraces where tenants could "serve a highball (if they dare)", though he noted the planners "had to omit provision for nudists" [1].

title: The Tenants Who Sued Over a 'White Ghetto'

place.label: Parkmerced towers near Juan Bautista Circle

hook: Two Parkmerced tenants, one Black and one white, argued that segregation hurt everyone. The U.S. Supreme Court agreed with them unanimously.
story: By the late 1960s Parkmerced, home to about 8,200 people, was overwhelmingly white in a city that was fast diversifying [1]. Two tenants filed complaints under the new Civil Rights Act of 1968. According to the Supreme Court, one was Black and one white [2]. They alleged that the owner had kept nonwhite applicants out by making it known they would not be welcome, manipulating the waiting list, delaying applications and using discriminatory standards [2]. Their injury, they said, was that they had lost the social benefits of living in an integrated community, missed business and professional advantages, and been stigmatized as residents of a "white ghetto" [2]. The Western Neighborhoods Project tells the story through Paul Trafficante, a white New Yorker who had come west after the war [1]. Could people who were not turned away themselves still sue? In Trafficante v. Metropolitan Life, decided December 7, 1972, Justice William O. Douglas wrote for the Court that they could [2]. Met Life settled and opened its apartments to all races, and Trafficante lived at Parkmerced until his death in 2001 [1].

title: Cabbage Fields to the Big E
hook: Two brothers turned cabbage fields into the fourth-largest apartment and shopping complex in the United States, and dotted it with palm trees.
story: In July 1949 the San Francisco News reported "a small city" rising west of 19th Avenue: Stonestown, the $23 million project of builders Ellis and Henry Stoneson [1]. On 67 acres of former cabbage fields and golf links, it would hold 783 rental units for 3,000 to 3,500 people, including four ten-story apartment houses of 90 flats each [1]. The Emporium department store, with its big "E" visible from 19th Avenue, opened its branch on July 16, 1952, and the center officially opened that November [1][2]. Walgreens, Woolworth's, Gallenkamp Shoes and the Red Chimney restaurant followed [1]. The Stonesons sold the open-air mall with celebrity ribbon-cuttings, parades and fairs, and were early adopters of palm trees on a grand scale [1]. Credit for the design is muddled: the Western Neighborhoods Project lists architect Angus McSweeney, while a 1951 News caption says Welton Becket designed the entire center [1]. In 1987 architect John Field added a second level of shops, a glass atrium and marble floors, and it reopened as Stonestown Galleria [1][2].

title: The College That Kept Moving West

place.label: San Francisco State campus, 1600 Holloway Avenue

hook: A teachers' school burned out in 1906 and squeezed onto Haight Street finally found room to grow on the windy shore of Lake Merced.
story: San Francisco State began in 1899 as Frederic Burk's State Normal School, a teacher-training college whose first graduating class was 36 young women [1]. The 1906 fire destroyed its Powell Street home, and Burk moved it to Haight and Buchanan streets [1]. It became San Francisco State College in 1935, and with nearly 1,000 students it bought land on the Lake Merced shoreline from the Spring Valley Water Company in 1937 [1]. World War II and arguments over land use stalled construction [1]. In 1948–49, a commemorative booklet recalled, the mayor, supervisors, legislators, Chamber of Commerce and press "united to develop a master plan for nine buildings" [1]. The Administration Building was finished in 1953, and under President J. Paul Leonard the college opened on 94 acres [1]. Classes began in fall 1953 and the campus was formally dedicated in October 1954 [2]. Today it covers about 144 acres [2].

title: Auden's Hundred Dollars

place.label: The Poetry Center, SF State Humanities Building

hook: W. H. Auden gave back half his speaking fee, and a professor turned it into one of the country's first public poetry reading series.
story: In 1954 W. H. Auden gave a talk at the brand-new San Francisco State College campus and returned half of his $200 honorarium [1][2]. English professor Ruth Witt-Diamant used the gift to found The Poetry Center, with advice from Kenneth Rexroth, Robert Duncan and Madeline Gleason, and from her late friend Dylan Thomas [1]. Its public reading series, one of the first in the United States, opened with Theodore Roethke in February 1954 [1]. Over the next years the center hosted some of the earliest recorded readings by poets of the San Francisco Renaissance, along with rare West Coast appearances by William Carlos Williams, Marianne Moore and Langston Hughes [1]. From 1955 it taped most readings, and in 1973 director Kathleen Fraser founded the American Poetry Archives to keep them [1]. The collection now holds about 5,000 hours of recordings, and the series is still running more than seventy years later [1].

title: The Longest Student Strike
hook: At 19th and Holloway, a linguist-turned-president climbed onto a strikers' sound truck to rip out the speaker wires, and a crowd snatched his tam o'shanter.
story: On November 6, 1968, the Black Students Union and the Third World Liberation Front called a strike at San Francisco State College, demanding a larger Black Studies program and the reinstatement of suspended instructor George Murray [1]. Their demands included Black, Asian American, American Indian and La Raza Studies departments within a College of Ethnic Studies [2]. After weeks of clashes the campus closed, and on November 26 President Robert Smith resigned [1]. English professor S. I. Hayakawa became acting president [1]. When the campus reopened on December 2, strikers parked a sound truck at the corner of 19th and Holloway. Hayakawa climbed on and tried to disconnect the speakers, and someone in the crowd pulled off his tam o'shanter [1]. In January about 350 teachers joined the picket lines [1]. An agreement on the fifteen demands was signed on March 20, 1969, and the strike ended the next day [1]. The result was the country's first College of Ethnic Studies [2].

title: A Zoo Poured in Concrete
hook: Depression-era builders wanted a zoo that could never burn. Decades later, renovators found concrete poured seven feet deep under the elephants.
story: Banker and parks commissioner Herbert Fleishhacker founded the zoo in 1929, and it carried his name until 1941, when at his suggestion it became the San Francisco Zoological Gardens [1][2]. Its first director, George Bistany, was an animal importer who got the job after delivering many of the first animals [1]. The zoo was largely built in the 1930s as a Works Progress Administration project, under zoologist Edmund Heller [1]. The rules were simple: it had to be fireproof, permanent and cheap to maintain, built only of reinforced concrete, with nothing blocking the view of the animals [1]. By 1940, at a cost of about $3.5 million, it had ten structures, including the Pachyderm and Lion Houses, an aviary, bear grottos and Monkey Island, with barless pits that were then considered innovative [1]. Monkey Island was demolished in 1995 [2]. Generations of west-side kids remember the Lion House at feeding time, when "hungry lions lunging for a dozen or so raw pot roasts" held them spellbound [3].

title: Two Women Paint Noah's Ark
hook: Two artists who came to sketch the animals spent four and a half years painting the flood's aftermath across the walls of a mothers' lounge.
story: Herbert and Mortimer Fleishhacker gave $50,000 for a Mother's Building in memory of their own mother, and it opened in 1925 beside the giant Fleishhacker Pool as a refuge for mothers and small children [1][2][3]. In the Depression, two San Francisco artists who had been sketching animals at the zoo, Helen Forbes and Dorothy Puccinelli, won New Deal support to decorate it [2][3]. Given free choice of subject, they picked Noah's Ark, after the waters recede [2][3]. Working in egg tempera for four and a half years, they finished in 1938 [3]. Elephants, white pelicans and donkeys make their way across the drying land while Noah stands among deer, a theme of renewal for a city in hard times [3]. Hoodline has described them as the largest set of egg tempera murals in the West [3]. Advocates note that every mural here was painted by women, unlike Coit Tower [3]. Moisture from fog and sea has damaged the walls, and the building has long been closed to the public while supporters push for restoration [2][3].

title: Koko, the Fireworks Child
hook: A gorilla born at the zoo on the Fourth of July learned her first signs from a Stanford graduate student in the Children's Zoo.
story: On July 4, 1971, a western lowland gorilla was born at the San Francisco Zoo and named Hanabi-ko, Japanese for "fireworks child" [1][2]. The world would know her as Koko. Stanford doctoral student Francine Patterson began teaching her sign language in 1972 [1]. Until June 1973 the lessons took place at the Children's Zoo exhibit, before Patterson and her partner Ronald Cohn moved the sessions to a trailer and then took Koko to Stanford [2]. Patterson and Cohn founded The Gorilla Foundation, and in 1979 Koko moved with them to the Santa Cruz Mountains [1]. According to the foundation, she came to use more than 1,000 signs and understand about 2,000 spoken English words [1]. National Geographic put her on its cover in October 1978 with a photo she took of herself in a mirror [1]. Scientists argued over whether she was really using language, and critics objected to her lifelong confinement [1][2]. She died in her sleep in June 2018, aged 46 [1].

title: The Pool Lifeguards Patrolled by Rowboat

place.label: Former Fleishhacker Pool site, now zoo parking

hook: The world's largest swimming tank held six million gallons of seawater. A 1971 storm broke one pipe, and the zoo wanted a parking lot.
story: Fleishhacker Pool opened on April 23, 1925: 1,000 feet long, 150 feet wide, filled with six million gallons of seawater and patrolled by up to two dozen lifeguards, some in rowboats [1]. Swimmer Ann Curtis set world records in it [1]. It was supposedly heated to seventy degrees, but everyone remembers the cold [1]. By the 1950s editorials called it a white elephant [1]. In January 1971 a storm damaged the outflow pipe to the ocean and the water became contaminated. The city tried fresh water for the first time and got algae instead [1]. The zoo campaigned to bury the pool. Director Saul Kitchener said that "its day has passed," and most of the land was earmarked for a parking lot [1]. A 1977 ballot measure to spend about a million dollars restoring it failed, and bulldozers began filling the pit in 1981 [1]. Old lifeguard Billy Nichols once asked Herbert Fleishhacker why he had built it so big. Fleishhacker told him to swim the length and back, then asked whether anyone had got in his way. "That's why I did it" [1].

title: Sixteen-Inch Guns Above the Surf
hook: The Army's secret weapon at Fort Funston could fire more than 25 miles out to sea. Today hang gliders float past its concrete casemates.
story: Battery Davis was begun in 1936 as part of the Harbor Defenses of San Francisco, the southern partner of Battery Townsley across the Golden Gate [1]. It held two 16-inch Navy guns, which arrived by rail from Mare Island in 1937 [2]. The National Park Service calls the 16-inch gun the Army's "secret weapon", able to shoot more than 25 miles into the Pacific [1]. After Pearl Harbor, soldiers worked 24-hour shifts in concrete lookouts, scanning sea and sky, and used listening devices to pick up the vibrations of ships or planes offshore [1]. The war swelled Fort Funston with 86 temporary barracks and other buildings [1]. The Japanese invasion never came [3]. By war's end the batteries were outdated and most of the post was torn down [1]. Nike missiles stood here from 1956 to 1963, and the land later went to the Golden Gate National Recreation Area [2]. Today the battery is a backdrop for hang gliders riding the cliff winds [3].

title: The Nobody Who Beat Ben Hogan
hook: Ben Hogan was congratulated on a record fifth U.S. Open. Then a municipal-course pro from Iowa birdied two of the last four holes.
story: In June 1955 the U.S. Open came to the Lake Course at the Olympic Club [1][2]. Ben Hogan, already a four-time champion, finished at 287 and appeared to have won a record fifth Open [1]. But Jack Fleck, 32, a municipal-course pro from Davenport, Iowa, in his first full year on tour, made two birdies on the last four holes to tie him [1]. Fleck forced the playoff by sinking an eight-foot birdie putt on the 18th [2]. There were only seven rounds under par all week, and Fleck shot three of them [1]. In the 18-hole playoff Hogan never led. He trailed by three after ten holes, fought back to one behind at the final tee, then his foot slipped and he drove into deep rough far to the left. It took him three strokes to get back to the fairway [1]. Fleck shot 69 to Hogan's 72 [1]. Adding to the sting, Fleck was reportedly playing clubs made by Hogan's own company [2]. Hogan never won another major [2].

title: From Parking Lot to Tiger's Playoff

place.label: Harding Park golf course, 99 Harding Road

hook: In 1998 the city's beloved public course was paved over with parked cars. Seven years later Tiger Woods won a playoff there against John Daly.
story: Harding Park opened in 1925, named for President Warren Harding, a keen golfer [2]. Byron Nelson won the Victory Open there in January 1944 and won again that December, when it had been renamed the San Francisco Open [2]. Johnny Miller learned the game there in the late 1950s. He biked over, fished in Lake Merced by the practice green and hustled middle-aged men for nickels [1]. The PGA Tour left after 1969, and budget cuts let the course decay [1][2]. It hit bottom in 1998, when it served as a parking lot for the U.S. Open at the neighboring Olympic Club [1][2]. Lawyer and former USGA president Sandy Tatum watched it "turning into a weed patch" and rallied the city and the Tour [2]. A $16 million restoration in 2002–03 followed [1][2]. In October 2005 Harding Park became the first municipal course to host a World Golf Championship [1]. Tiger Woods, who remembered it as "basically a clover field", beat John Daly on the third playoff hole [1][2].

title: The Lake That Nearly Drained Away
hook: Lake Merced was once stocked with a quarter of a million fish a year. Then golf courses and cemeteries pumped the aquifer and its boathouse went dark.
story: In the 1950s the state utilities commission gave San Francisco's Recreation and Park Department control of Lake Merced's surface. The conditions were strict: keep the drinking water potable, keep the level up, allow no swimming and no gasoline engines [1]. The city built a first-class urban fishery. At its height stocking reached 250,000 fish [1]. But heavy postwar pumping of the Westside Aquifer by golf courses, cities and cemeteries drew the lake down [1]. As the water fell, stocking all but stopped. The Boat House, once a busy restaurant and bar, closed, and fishing piers were left standing over tule-choked banks [1]. Better management of the aquifer and occasional added water helped the lake start rising again from about 1990 [2]. By 2004 angler Tony Van Houten could report a lake "on the rebound", thanks to CalTrout, the Lake Merced Task Force and the Friends of Lake Merced. There was a new fishing pier, and the state planned to plant 50,000 fish that year [1].
